extracted.intended_audience: educated general public; teachers and public-health practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory guidance and scientific observations about school-room ventilation (definition, pollutants, physiological effects, and practical implications) embedded in a Popular Science Monthly article; also includes a preceding discussion-classification of visual hallucinations and illusions in sane persons. Primarily actionable for teachers, school administrators, and public-health officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ventilation
rubrics_metrics.description: "VENTILATION is the supply of fresh air to an apartment, and the removal of impure or vitiated air therefrom."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the dual objective of ventilation: supply fresh oxygen and remove impurities (vitiated air).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of pure air
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pure air consists of a mechanical mixture of about four fifths nitrogen and one fifth oxygen, with traces of ammonia, and about one part in two thousand of carbonic-acid gas (CO2)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline composition provided to explain why ventilation must maintain oxygen levels and dilute other gases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-person breathing rates and volumes (school context)
rubrics_metrics.description: A full-grown person breathes about twenty times per minute and takes in over twenty cubic inches of air at each inspiration; boys and girls somewhat less volume but faster (about 25 breaths/min). In a two-hour session each person breathes nearly twenty-five cubic feet of air; in a school of forty pupils about one thousand cubic feet will be inhaled every two hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifies classroom air turnover needs and scales per-classroom pollutant generation; useful for estimating ventilation rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxygen consumption and CO2 production per class
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxygen to the amount of nearly five per cent of the quantity inhaled disappears at every breath — about twenty cubic inches per minute per individual — representing about fifty cubic feet of oxygen consumed for a school of forty pupils in two hours; similarly, breathing produces about forty-five cubic feet of carbonic-acid gas (CO2) in two hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives numerical basis for understanding accumulation of CO2 and the need to supply fresh air to replace consumed oxygen.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common school-room air impurities
rubrics_metrics.description: Air impurities usually found in the school-room: carbonic oxide (CO), carbonic-acid gas (CO2), ammonia (NH3), sulphur (S), sulphuretted hydrogen (H2S), aqueous vapor, organic matters, inorganic matters, epithelial cells, and animal exhalations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates gaseous and particulate contaminants that ventilation must control; distinguishes those especially relevant to schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbon monoxide is the most toxic common impurity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most toxic of all these is undoubtedly carbon monoxide (CO)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes CO is produced by incomplete combustion (stoves) and can enter rooms through stove doors, defective flues, or leaks; it is tasteless, colorless, and inodorous, so cannot be detected by senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stove-heating hazard and leakage pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: In schools heated by stoves, products of combustion (sulphur, carbonic oxide, carbonic-acid gas) may find their way into the room through the stove door, seams, cracks, defective joints in flues, or downward/lateral air-currents in the flue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical warning that stove-heated classrooms are at risk of combustion gas ingress; suggests inspecting seals, flues, and accounting for downdrafts and open windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 mixing behavior and density effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Although CO2 is heavier than air, "the mixture of gases in free communication, however their density, takes place rapidly, and is homogeneous" — so CO2 percentage is about the same in all parts of the room; as CO2 increases the density of the air increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that CO2 will not simply 'settle' but will evenly mix; rising CO2 increases air density and impairs gas exchange in lungs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and cognitive effects of elevated CO2
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess CO2 circulating through the brain produces drowsiness, dizziness, dull headache, an inability to fix the attention, a dislike for application, a weakening of the memory, and a general torpor of the intellectual powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames CO2 accumulation as directly harmful to learning and teacher performance; motivates regular ventilation to sustain cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diurnal timing consideration: post-meal CO2 increase
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhalation of carbonic-acid gas is very much increased — often nearly doubled — during active digestion; as the fullest meal is at dinner, CO2 exhalation is greatest during the early part of the afternoon, and therefore ventilation needs more attention at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical scheduling note: increase ventilation attention/effort in early afternoon sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic airborne matter and infection risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Epithelial cells and other organic matters arise from the body (desquamation from skin, mouth, pharynx, bronchi); these float in air and are inhaled, lodging in the respiratory tract. In infectious diseases (diphtheria, scarlatina, smallpox, measles) epithelial scales increase and carry infection, so preventing their accumulation via ventilation reduces transplantable infection centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues ventilation reduces airborne particulate infection risk by removing suspended infectious material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal exhalations (human odors) concentrate at room top and are rapidly prostrating
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal exhalations are volatile and light, rise to the highest portions of the room, and if not allowed to escape accumulate there, saturating air from above downward; they are the most perceptible, offensive, and rapidly prostrating noxious matters in fouled school-room air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates importance of ventilators or openings high in the room (roof/ceiling level) to remove concentrated odors; anecdote: removing tiles at high level eliminated odor immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation as removal mechanism for suspended organic and odorous matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Since epithelial scales and other organic matters float in the air and follow its currents, they are removed by ventilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects the mechanics of airflow to infection control and odor removal; supports deliberate airflow design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confinement in vitiated air may predispose to tubercle (historic claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Dr. Routh: 'if an animal be kept confined in a narrow, closed apartment, so that the air supplied is always more or less vitiated by the carbonic acid which it expires, however well fed that animal may be, tubercle (consumption) will be developed in about three months.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical experimental claim used to underline potential chronic health risks of poor ventilation (interpret cautiously given historical context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and clinical features of visions (sane persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visions' weirdness lies in their sudden appearance, vividness while present, and sudden departure. They may be highly distinct yet the person does not mistake them for reality; they can be experienced by sane persons in normal health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive diagnostic characteristics helpful for distinguishing transient visions in sane individuals from other psychopathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: hallucination vs illusion vs hybrid cases
rubrics_metrics.description: "A convenient distinction is made between hallucinations and illusions. Hallucinations are defined as appearances wholly due to fancy; illusions, as misrepresentations of objects actually seen." There is also a hybrid case: direct vision or induced vision may be interpreted fancifully, yielding three cases: (1) simple hallucination (induced vision rightly observed), (2) simple illusion (direct vision fancifully observed), (3) hybrid (induced vision fancifully observed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a three-part classificatory rubric for analyzing anomalous perceptual experiences; useful for clinical/phenomenological description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of illusion formation (attention and eye-movement factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first essential element in their construction is the smallness of the area upon which attention is directed at any instant, so the eye must move much before it has traveled over every part of the object. The eye wanders in devious curves; direction depends on muscular motion, idiosyncrasy, mood, and current associations. Imagination dwells on a fancy picture; incongruities are disregarded and deficiencies supplied by the fantasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains psychological-perceptual processes (attention narrowing, eye movements, associative filling-in) that produce illusions and fire-faces; supports experimental/phenomenological investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visions as patchworks / composite portraits from recollections
rubrics_metrics.description: Visions, like dreams, are often mere patchworks built up of bits of recollections; blended memories can create composite faces with novel individuality. Superposition (lantern/photographic) analogies are used to show how images are retained, discarded, or supplied by imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts for the diversity and novelty of phantasmagoria via combination of remembered elements; suggests experimental analogies for study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predisposing conditions for visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of fasting, want of sleep, solitary musing, protracted wakefulness, and spiritual discipline (self-control, self-mortification) are conducive to visions; social amusements reduce them; visionary tendency is often hereditary and may be characteristic of families or races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists behavioral and social factors that increase or decrease likelihood of visionary experiences; useful for risk/context assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and occupational factors in prominent visionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolation of life, intense solitary intellectual activity, and the overwrought brains of great men may develop visionary tendencies; a visionary temperament manifests in certain historical periods and national epochs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame for understanding occurrence of visions among eminent individuals as partly social/occupational rather than purely pathological.
